Saturday evening. Sahil stayed after the workshop at the community hall, laptop open, when Bidisha, a data analyst who ran the session, came to look. "You have a project?"

He nodded and turned the screen: a chart of local bus delays built from a public dataset, made over three weekends while he kept his job. She scrolled, asked what he meant by one column, and said, "Your method is sound. The chart hides the busiest hour. Fix that." A second professional, who was passing, added a comment about labels.

Sahil's stomach flipped as he listened, but he took notes. Riding the bus home, he thought: I didn't have to quit anything to find out if I like this. And I do.

qa.a: Bidisha probably sees a keen beginner with a sound method, and saying the chart hides the busiest hour was a way of helping him improve.

Joseph,
You asked what happened with the data project, so here's the update.
While still at the textile firm, I spent six weekends on a small project: I took the city's public data on bus routes and ridership and tried to find which routes were overcrowded at peak hours. I cleaned the data, made three charts and wrote a two-page summary.
Then I sent it to two people I'd met at a meetup: an analyst at a transport company and a data lead at a bank. The analyst said my cleaning was careful but my charts tried to show too much at once. The data lead said my conclusions went further than the data allowed.
Honestly, it stung for a day. But I enjoyed every weekend, even the boring cleaning. So now I know I actually like this work, and I know two things to fix.
Next project: smaller, sharper charts.
Jasleen

"Jaya, you asked on this call how I knew data was for me. I didn't, at first. So I, Gurpreet, tested it.
I was doing sales support at a phone company. I liked numbers but had no idea if I'd like them all day. Quitting to find out felt crazy.
So on weekday nights I took a public dataset on air quality in Indian cities and tried to answer one question: which months are worst, and does it differ north to south? It took me a month of evenings.
Then I showed it to two people from my cousin's office who work in analytics. One said my analysis was solid but my writing was confusing. The other asked a question I couldn't answer, and I found I really wanted to find out.
That was the moment I knew. Not from the praise. From wanting to go back and dig more."

qa.q: What question did Gurpreet's project try to answer?
qa.a: Which months are worst for air quality, and whether it differs north to south.

qa.q: What did Gurpreet feel when the second person asked an unanswerable question?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt curious and eager, really wanting to go back and find out.

qa.q: What else could Gurpreet do after showing the project?
qa.a: Gurpreet could fix the confusing writing and answer the open question, then share the improved version to see if the interest still holds.

qa.a: They might be impressed that someone in sales support did careful analysis on their own time and ask sharp questions.
